name: Person Bouncing Ball
baseMeaning: A person bouncing ball emoji: a figure crouched with one hand pushing a basketball down to the floor.
tldr: Person Bouncing Ball ⛹️: showing off a sport, usually to claim competence.

contextMeanings.meaning: In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — showing off a sport, usually to claim competence — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.
The plain reading: a figure crouched with one hand pushing a basketball down to the floor. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Announcing you are heading to the gym ⛹️

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as showing off a sport, usually to claim competence.
contextMeanings.example: Joking about your terrible free throws ⛹️

contextMeanings.meaning: Used sarcastically it is the gesture with the deadpan delivery: showing off a sport, usually to claim competence, said without believing any of it.

platformNotes.note: In TikTok comments ⛹️ is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays showing off a sport, usually to claim competence, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack ⛹️ lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for announcing you are heading to the gym, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord ⛹️ is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its showing off a sport, usually to claim competence reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter ⛹️ does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like joking about your terrible free throws. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Person Bouncing Ball ⛹️ renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like announcing you are heading to the gym is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

generationalNotes.note: Older senders use ⛹️ in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the showing off a sport, usually to claim competence subtext in it.

Gen Z reaches for ⛹️ to do the work of announcing you are heading to the gym, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is showing off a sport, usually to claim competence.

Millennials tend to send ⛹️ deliberately, usually for something like joking about your terrible free throws, and they read showing off a sport, usually to claim competence into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses ⛹️ literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read showing off a sport, usually to claim competence into it than younger senders are.

warnings.title: ⛹️ and 🏀 get swapped
warnings.description: The Basketball 🏀 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the ball is the object being played with, the figure is the person handling it. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take ⛹️ as something else fairly often: it gets taken for genuine athletic pride when it is usually a joke about being bad at the sport — the crouch is the giveaway. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: ⛹️ Person Bouncing Ball Emoji Meaning and How to Use It
seoDescription: What ⛹️ means when people send it, the person bouncing ball reading, and how to answer it without guessing.

longForm.overview:
What follows is the useful part: the two things the person bouncing ball is actually for (announcing you are heading to the gym and joking about your terrible free throws), the reading it gets when it is not what the sender meant, and the five tone pages that sit under this one.

There is not a lot to the picture. ⛹️ is a figure crouched with one hand pushing a basketball down to the floor, added in Unicode 13.0 and filed under sport. What it does in a message is carry a meaning — here, showing off a sport, usually to claim competence — without anyone having to write it out.

That plain reading is the one most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one. The picture is doing the same work as the sentence it replaces, and it lands first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets taken for genuine athletic pride when it is usually a joke about being bad at the sport — the crouch is the giveaway. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🏀 Basketball: the ball is the object being played with, the figure is the person handling it. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

There are five tone versions of this emoji, and they are not copies of this page. Each one describes the same gesture from inside a different group, because a tone is read as a signal about the sender before the sentence is read.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
The common uses are announcing you are heading to the gym and joking about your terrible free throws. The first one is about speed — the picture replaces the explanation, and it lands before the words would have. The second is about tone — the sentence stands on its own, and the emoji is there to change how it reads.

The same emoji in three rooms: a family thread, a work channel, and a dating app. In the first it closes a conversation, in the second it hands something over, in the third it is a joke with an eyebrow raised. The drawing never changes; the expectation of the reader does.

That is also the reason the skin-tone variants are written as their own pages rather than as one page with a table of swatches. A tone is not a setting, and it is read differently.

Look at how often ⛹️ is used to avoid typing. A question goes out, a question comes back, and in between there is a single picture standing in for an answer that would have taken a sentence. It reads as "showing off a sport, usually to claim competence", which is fine until it is not.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Watch the picker, and watch the thread. ⛹️ is easy to send when 🏀 Basketball was meant — the ball is the object being played with, the figure is the person handling it. And the emoji has no business being the whole reply to somebody who has just told you something bad: it reads as "showing off a sport, usually to claim competence", which is about the gesture rather than about them.

The problem is not the emoji, it is the message underneath it. ⛹️ gets taken for genuine athletic pride when it is usually a joke about being bad at the sport — the crouch is the giveaway, and the drift happens silently. Nobody notices that the meaning changed, because the change was in a picture.

Nor is it a good opener with a stranger. The drawing is cold, and person bouncing ball gestures have collected a faintly superior edge from being used to reply to other people for years.

Professional settings are the other place to leave it alone. Put ⛹️ next to somebody's performance, or in a first note to a client, and showing off a sport, usually to claim competence is the note it reads as — a note that costs more in a workplace than in a group chat.
longForm.howToReply:
Matching works when the message was a reaction: send ⛹️ back and the tone is confirmed without a word. It does not work when the message was aimed at you. A request, a handover, a nudge — those want a sentence, because two gestures in a row leave the question open.

If you cannot tell how the person bouncing ball was meant, read the line above it instead. ⛹️ gets taken for genuine athletic pride when it is usually a joke about being bad at the sport — the crouch is the giveaway; the sentence underneath is the part that disambiguates it.

Warmth needs words next to the picture. Something like announcing you are heading to the gym sent with ⛹️ on its own is a coin toss between showing off a sport, usually to claim competence and something sharper, and the sender never gets to pick which one landed.

faqs.question: What does ⛹️ mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between ⛹️ and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under person bouncing ball show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does ⛹️ mean in text?
faqs.answer: ⛹️ is used for showing off a sport, usually to claim competence. The drawing shows a figure crouched with one hand pushing a basketball down to the floor, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between ⛹️ and 🏀?
faqs.answer: The ball is the object being played with, the figure is the person handling it. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is ⛹️ rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as showing off a sport, usually to claim competence, but it gets taken for genuine athletic pride when it is usually a joke about being bad at the sport — the crouch is the giveaway. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as showing off a sport, usually to claim competence, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

It gets taken for genuine athletic pride when it is usually a joke about being bad at the sport — the crouch is the giveaway more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.
